steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a software engineering paper about what success means to open source contributors. It should argue that success in OSS is more than code, state our research question, briefly describe our interview and survey study and main finding, and outline the paper.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Success in Open Source Software (OSS) is about much more than code contributions. But there is a common misperception that programming skills are what determine success in OSS. You can see this perception in the way projects highlight programming metrics on their sites (for example number of lines of code or number of commits) and in the way they decide on advancement in roles (for example what you need to become a core member/maintainer or to get commit access), and all of these are code-centric concepts. Academic research has also added to this misperception, maybe without meaning to, because past studies have mostly focused on code. For example, many papers recognize the “onion model” as the way that contributors join, grow, and get commit access to the code repository.

But OSS contributors are a heterogeneous group. They have different talents, skills, career goals, and motivations. Some of them do various non-code activities (like advocacy, technical writing, translation, project management) and they follow a different pathway than the well-known “onion model”. OSS communities involve a lot more players than only their “code warriors”, so success has to be recognized as more than just how much code someone produces.

- Definitions of success matter
  - shape personal/professional choices and how we evaluate others: education, where to work, project involvement, career attainment, life satisfaction
  - OSS literature: mostly immediate motivation to join and continue; perceptions of success overlooked
  - success = long-term goals, imagined career future; influences commitment and behavior
  - need to understand factors; how else to support people who don't fit onion model?
- RQ: What does it mean to be successful in OSS?
- Method: 27 interviews with recognized successful contributors; Dries et al. success model; survey of 193 contributors for triangulation
- Results: multi-faceted; objective (money, amount of contribution) + subjective (recognition, satisfaction); von Krogh quote; reflect and make OSS more diverse
- Outline of sections II–IX

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Success in Open Source Software (OSS) is about much more than code contributions. But there is a common misperception that programming skills are what determine success in OSS. You can see this perception in the way projects highlight programming metrics on their sites (for example number of lines of code or number of commits) and in the way they decide on advancement in roles (for example what you need to become a core member/maintainer or to get commit access), and all of these are code-centric concepts. Academic research has also added to this misperception, maybe without meaning to, because past studies have mostly focused on code. For example, many papers recognize the “onion model” as the way that contributors join, grow, and get commit access to the code repository.

But OSS contributors are a heterogeneous group. They have different talents, skills, career goals, and motivations. Some of them do various non-code activities (like advocacy, technical writing, translation, project management) and they follow a different pathway than the well-known “onion model”. OSS communities involve a lot more players than only their “code warriors”, so success has to be recognized as more than just how much code someone produces.

The way people define success has an impact on the choices they make in their personal and professional lives, and on how they evaluate other people. Definitions of success can affect things like educational choices, decisions on where to work, involvement in projects, career attainment, life satisfaction, and so on. So far the OSS literature has mostly looked at the immediate motivation to join OSS and to continue, and it has overlooked how contributors perceive success. Perceptions of success represent long-term goals and an imagined future career, and this influences commitment and human behavior. So it is important to understand in a comprehensive way the many factors behind what success means for an individual in OSS. Without this understanding, how can OSS communities support all the different people whose future goals and pathways don't fit the usual onion model career mold?

In this study we address the fundamental research question: What does it mean to be successful in OSS?

To answer it, we interviewed 27 OSS contributors who are recognized as successful figures in their communities. We analyzed the interviews qualitatively using the “success model” proposed by Dries et al.. Then we triangulated the results with data from a survey of 193 OSS contributors.

Our results show that OSS contributors define success in ways that are multi-faceted and nuanced. Success includes objective measures (like monetary compensation and amount of contribution) and also subjective ones (like recognition in the community and satisfaction). In the words of von Krogh: “ Occasionally, humans also make elaborate detours, strive for bigger things in life, and undertake long voyages to find the gold at the end of the rainbow.” So it is time to reflect on what we consider success in OSS, and on how we can help make OSS more diverse by finding different ways to support people with various backgrounds and different definitions of success.

In this paper, Section II introduces the definition of career success and the theoretical success model we use, Section III our research method and Section IV the results. Sections V & VI discuss the implications of our results, and then come related work, limitations, and conclusions in Sections VII, VIII, and Section IX.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Success in Open Source Software (OSS) encompasses much more than code contributions. However, there is a widespread misperception that programming skills determine success in OSS [1]. This perception shows in how projects highlight programming-related metrics on their sites (e.g., number of lines of code, number of commits) and in how they determine advancement in roles (e.g., what it takes to become a core member/maintainer or gain commit access)—all code-centric concepts [2,3]. Academic research has also, perhaps inadvertently, contributed to this misperception, since past studies have largely been code-focused. For instance, numerous papers recognize the “onion model” as the mechanism through which contributors join, grow, and receive commit access to the code repository [4,5,6].

OSS contributors, however, are a heterogeneous group, with different talents, skills, career goals, and motivations [7,8,9,10]. Some perform a variety of non-code activities (e.g., advocacy, technical writing, translation, project management) [1,11] and follow a different pathway than the acclaimed “onion model” [12,13,1]. Since OSS communities involve many more players than just their “code warriors”, success must be recognized as more than the quantity of code one produces.

How people define success affects the choices they make in their personal and professional lives and how they evaluate others. Definitions of success can influence educational choices, decisions about where to work, project involvement, career attainment, life satisfaction, and so on [14]. Thus far, the OSS literature has mostly investigated the immediate motivation to join and continue in OSS [7,8,9,10], overlooking contributors’ perceptions of success. Perceptions of success represent long-term goals and an imagined career future [15,16], which influence commitment [17] and human behavior [15,16]. It is therefore important to comprehensively understand the many factors underlying what success means to an individual in OSS. Without such an understanding, how can OSS communities support the diverse individuals whose future goals and pathways do not fit the typical onion model career mold?

In this study, we tackle the fundamental research question: What does it mean to be successful in OSS?

To answer this question, we interviewed 27 OSS contributors who are recognized as successful figures in their communities. We qualitatively analyzed the interviews using the “success model” proposed by Dries et al. [18], and then triangulated our results with data from a survey of 193 OSS contributors.

Our results indicate that OSS contributors define success in multi-faceted and nuanced ways. Success includes objective measures (e.g., monetary compensations, amounts of contribution) as well as subjective ones (e.g., recognition in the community, satisfaction). In the words of von Krogh [9]: “ Occasionally, humans also make elaborate detours, strive for bigger things in life, and undertake long voyages to find the gold at the end of the rainbow.” It is thus time to reflect on what we consider success in OSS, and on how we can make OSS more diverse by finding different ways to support individuals with various backgrounds and distinct definitions of success.

In this paper, we introduce the definition of career success and the theoretical success model we use in Section II, followed by our research method and results in Sections III and IV. Sections V & VI discuss the implications of our results, followed by related work, limitations, and conclusions in Sections VII, VIII, and Section IX.
